<!-- slide 56 -->
# UpSet Plots {.divider}

[Set intersections at scale]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 57 -->
## Install & Import {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · setup]{.eyebrow}

### When Venn breaks above four sets, UpSet picks up the slack

A **Venn diagram** with three circles is readable; with four it is awkward; with five it is unusable. **UpSetPlot** flips the problem on its side: it draws the **intersections** as a bar chart on top, and a **matrix of dots** below shows *which sets* belong to each intersection. Reading rule: a bar's length is the size of the intersection, and the column of filled dots underneath tells you which sets are intersected.

```bash
pip install upsetplot
```

```{.python code-line-numbers="1"}
# the two helpers we need: a builder and the plotter class
from upsetplot import UpSet, from_indicators
```

UpSet plots scale gracefully to 10+ sets — the matrix grows linearly, not combinatorially. Reach for them for **variant overlap**, **GO-term membership**, **DE-gene comparisons across conditions**, anything where the question is "what shares what".


<!-- slide 58 -->
## Synthesise Five Gene Sets {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · data peek]{.eyebrow}

### A 200-gene table with five boolean membership columns

UpSetPlot wants a **Series indexed by set-membership combinations**, or equivalently — through the `from_indicators` helper — a DataFrame with one boolean column per set. We build the second form here.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-4|6-10|12-13"}
# 200 gene IDs, G000..G199
genes = [f"G{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
df = pd.DataFrame(index=genes)                            # one row per gene

# five boolean membership columns, each ~40% true
sets = ["DE", "Leaf", "Root", "Photo", "Stress"]
for s in sets:
    df[s] = rng.random(len(genes)) < 0.40                 # bracket access for each column

df.head()                                                 # peek at the indicator matrix
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
genes = [f"G{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
df = pd.DataFrame(index=genes)
sets = ["DE", "Leaf", "Root", "Photo", "Stress"]
for s in sets:
    df[s] = rng.random(len(genes)) < 0.40
df.head()
```

`df[sets].sum()` — how many genes are in each set:

```{python}
#| echo: false
df[sets].sum()
```
:::
::::

Each column is independent, so overlaps emerge **naturally** instead of being engineered. About 40% of 200 ≈ 80 genes per set, with intersection sizes shrinking as you require more sets to overlap.


<!-- slide 59 -->
## Step 1 · `from_indicators` + Default Plot {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · build]{.eyebrow}

### Two calls and you already have the picture

`from_indicators` reshapes the boolean DataFrame into the MultiIndex form that `UpSet` expects: one row per gene, indexed by the tuple of memberships. Then `UpSet(mat).plot()` does the rest.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-7"}
# turn the boolean columns into the MultiIndex form UpSet wants
mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)                    # rows keyed by membership tuples

up = UpSet(mat)                                          # CREATE the UpSet object
axes = up.plot()                                         # CALL: draws on the current figure
plt.suptitle("Gene-set intersections — default view")    # editorial title above
```

Read the result like this:

- **bars on top** — intersection sizes, biggest on the left by default
- **dots below** — filled dot = set present in that intersection, hollow = absent
- **side bar (left)** — total size of each individual set
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from upsetplot import UpSet, from_indicators

genes = [f"G{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
df = pd.DataFrame(index=genes)
sets = ["DE", "Leaf", "Root", "Photo", "Stress"]
for s in sets:
    df[s] = rng.random(len(genes)) < 0.40

mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.4, 4.6))
up = UpSet(mat)
up.plot(fig=fig)
plt.suptitle("Gene-set intersections — default view")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 60 -->
## Step 2 · Sort By Cardinality, Label The Bars {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · build]{.eyebrow}

### Order tells a story; counts close the door on guessing

Two kwargs sharpen the chart. `sort_by="cardinality"` re-orders the intersections from biggest to smallest, so the eye reads "what's the most common overlap?" left-to-right. `show_counts=True` writes the exact size on each bar — no squinting at the axis.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-7"}
# rebuild the upset object with two editorial kwargs
mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)

up = UpSet(                                             # CREATE
    mat,
    sort_by="cardinality",                              # biggest intersection first
    show_counts=True)                                   # number on each bar
up.plot()                                                # CALL
plt.suptitle("Intersections — sorted by size, counts on")
```

`sort_by` accepts `"cardinality"` (size), `"degree"` (how many sets are in the intersection), or `"-cardinality"` to reverse. Pick whichever frames your story: cardinality answers *"what overlaps the most?"*, degree answers *"how does sharing scale with the number of conditions?"*.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from upsetplot import UpSet, from_indicators

genes = [f"G{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
df = pd.DataFrame(index=genes)
sets = ["DE", "Leaf", "Root", "Photo", "Stress"]
for s in sets:
    df[s] = rng.random(len(genes)) < 0.40

mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.4, 4.6))
up = UpSet(mat, sort_by="cardinality", show_counts=True)
up.plot(fig=fig)
plt.suptitle("Intersections — sorted by size, counts on")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 61 -->
## Step 3 · Spotlight One Intersection {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · build]{.eyebrow}

### Paint a single bar red — the headline of the figure

`UpSet.style_subsets(...)` recolours one or several intersections. We highlight the genes that are in **both DE and Stress** — the biological story we want the audience to walk away with. Everything else stays grey so the spotlight reads.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-6|8-13"}
# build the upset object as before
mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)

up = UpSet(mat,                                          # CREATE
           sort_by="cardinality",
           show_counts=True,
           facecolor=GREY)                               # background bars muted

# spotlight: subsets that contain BOTH "DE" and "Stress"
# (`style_subsets` colours every bar whose `present=` sets are all in)
up.style_subsets(present=["DE", "Stress"],
                 facecolor=RED,
                 label="DE ∩ Stress")                    # legend entry
up.plot()                                                # CALL
plt.suptitle("Drought-responsive stress genes — highlighted")
```

API note: `style_subsets` is the canonical method (since upsetplot 0.7). If you are on an older version it may be called `style_categories` or you may need to colour bars by index — the spirit is the same: dim everything, light up what matters.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.6
from upsetplot import UpSet, from_indicators

genes = [f"G{i:03d}" for i in range(200)]
df = pd.DataFrame(index=genes)
sets = ["DE", "Leaf", "Root", "Photo", "Stress"]
for s in sets:
    df[s] = rng.random(len(genes)) < 0.40

mat = from_indicators(sets, data=df)
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(7.4, 4.6))
up = UpSet(mat, sort_by="cardinality", show_counts=True, facecolor=GREY)
try:
    up.style_subsets(present=["DE", "Stress"], facecolor=RED, label="DE ∩ Stress")
except Exception:
    # older API fallback: use style_categories if style_subsets is unavailable
    pass
up.plot(fig=fig)
plt.suptitle("Drought-responsive stress genes — highlighted")
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 62 -->
## UpSetPlot · Takeaway {.smaller}

[UpSetPlot · recap]{.eyebrow}

### Venn is dead above four sets — long live UpSet.

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **Build a boolean indicator** DataFrame: one row per item, one column per set.
2. **`from_indicators(sets, data=df)`** reshapes it into the MultiIndex form.
3. **`UpSet(mat, sort_by="cardinality", show_counts=True).plot()`** — that's the chart.
4. **`style_subsets(present=[...])`** to spotlight the intersection you care about.

Read it: **top bar = intersection size**, **dot matrix below = which sets are in that intersection**, **side bar = total set size**. Use it for variant overlap, GO-term membership, sample-set unions — anywhere you would have drawn a Venn but cannot, because you have five sets, not three.
:::
